title: Everyone but me
statement: For each position i in an array of n integers, compute the product of all the other elements (every element except the one at i). Do not use division, and values may be zero.
input: One line of n integers.
output: n integers: the product of the others for each position.

examples.why: For 1 the others multiply to 2*3*4=24, and so on.
Only the position of the 0 gets a non-zero result (2*3=6).

hints: The product of others equals (product to the left) times (product to the right).
Build left products in one pass, then multiply by a running right product in a second pass.
approach: Fill the output with prefix products (product of everything left of i). Then sweep from the right keeping a running suffix product and multiply it in.
complexity: O(n) time, O(1) extra space besides the output

title: Next lock code
statement: A combination lock shows a sequence of digits. Rearrange them into the next larger arrangement in dictionary (lexicographic) order, using the same multiset of numbers. If the sequence is already the largest possible, wrap around to the smallest arrangement (sorted ascending).
input: One line of n integers.
output: The next arrangement as n integers.

examples.why: Pivot 1 swaps with 2, and the tail becomes ascending: 2 1 3.
Fully descending is the largest, so wrap to ascending.

hints: Find the rightmost position where a[i] < a[i+1]; everything after it is descending.
Swap a[i] with the smallest larger value to its right, then reverse the suffix.
approach: Scan from the right for the first index i with a[i] < a[i+1]. Swap a[i] with the rightmost element greater than it, then reverse the suffix after i. If no such i exists, just reverse the whole array.

title: Count the mirror pieces
statement: Count how many substrings of a string are palindromes. Substrings are counted by position, so two equal pieces at different places count separately, and every single character counts.
input: One lowercase string.
output: One integer.

examples.why: a, a, a, aa, aa, aaa.
5 singles, aba, bab, aba, and ababa.

hints: Every palindrome has a centre: a character or a gap between two characters.
Expand outwards from each of the 2n-1 centres while the ends match.
approach: For each of the 2n-1 possible centres expand left and right while the characters are equal, counting each successful expansion. The total of all expansions is the answer.

title: Stretches with an exact total
statement: Count the number of consecutive stretches (non-empty subarrays) of an integer array whose elements add up to exactly k. Values may be negative or zero, so a simple sliding window will not work.
input: Line 1: n integers; line 2: the integer k.
output: One integer.

examples.why: [1,1] at two different positions.
[3,4], [3,1,3], and the whole array.

hints: A stretch sum equals prefix[j] - prefix[i].
So for each j count earlier prefixes equal to prefix[j] - k, using a hash map of counts.
approach: Track the running prefix sum and a map from prefix value to how many times it has occurred (starting with 0 once). For each new prefix p add count[p-k] to the answer, then record p.

title: Longest run of tickets
statement: Raffle tickets are drawn in random order. Find the length of the longest group of drawn numbers that form consecutive integers (like 7, 8, 9, 10), regardless of the order they were drawn. Do it faster than sorting.
input: One line of n integers (duplicates possible).
output: One integer.

examples.why: 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 are all present.
A single number is a run of length 1.

hints: Put all numbers in a hash set.
Only start counting from numbers whose predecessor x-1 is absent.
approach: Insert everything into a set. For each x with x-1 missing, extend upward while x+1 exists and track the longest length. Each number is visited at most twice overall.

title: Pairs with a fixed gap
statement: Count the distinct pairs of values (x, y) from an array with y - x = k, where k ≥ 0. Pairs are counted by value, not position; for k = 0 the pair (x, x) needs x to appear at least twice.
input: Line 1: n integers; line 2: the integer k.
output: One integer.

examples.why: Only the value 1 repeats, so one pair (1,1).

hints: Count occurrences with a hash map.
For k>0 count values x such that x+k is also present; k=0 is a special case.
approach: Build a frequency map. If k is 0, count values with frequency at least 2; otherwise count values x for which x+k is a key in the map.

title: Balanced trios
statement: Each item in a list has a signed weight. Count the distinct value-triples (a, b, c) that can be picked from three different positions and add up to zero. Triples with the same three values count once, no matter the order or which positions were used.
input: One line of n integers.
output: One integer.

examples.why: Only (0,0,0), though many position choices exist.

hints: Sort first, fix the smallest element, and search for the other two with two pointers.
Skip duplicate values for the fixed element and after finding a trio.
approach: Sort the array. For each index i (skipping repeated values), run left/right pointers over the rest: move left up when the sum is too small, right down when too large, and record and skip duplicates on a hit.
complexity: O(n^2) time, O(1) extra space besides sorting

title: At most twice
statement: A sorted list of tags may repeat values many times. Edit it so that each value appears at most twice, keeping the order, and print the resulting list.
input: One line of n sorted integers.
output: The reduced list.

examples.why: The third 1 is dropped.
Only two 4s survive.

hints: Compare the candidate with the element two places back in the kept list.
If they are equal, a third copy would appear, so skip it.
approach: Keep a write index k. For each element x, if k < 2 or x differs from the element at position k-2 of the kept part, write it and increment k.

title: Shortest stretch that is enough
statement: Each day a battery gathers a positive amount of charge. Find the shortest run of consecutive days whose total charge is at least a target, and print its length, or 0 if even all days together are not enough.
input: Line 1: n positive integers; line 2: the target.
output: One integer.

examples.why: 4+4 = 8 uses two days.
Total is 3 < 10.

hints: All values are positive, so the sum grows when the window grows.
Shrink from the left as long as the sum stays ≥ target.
approach: Grow the right end adding values; while the sum meets the target, record the window length and shrink from the left. Positive values make this two-pointer scan valid.
edgeCases: target met by a single element

title: Few flavours stretch
statement: A conveyor belt carries candies, each shown as a lowercase letter for its flavour. Find the longest run of consecutive candies containing at most k different flavours.
input: Line 1: the string; line 2: the integer k.
output: One integer.

examples.why: "aabb" or "bbcc".
Every run with one flavour has length 1.

hints: Track counts of each flavour in the window.
Shrink from the left while there are more than k distinct flavours.
approach: Slide a window with a count map. After adding the right character, while the map has more than k keys remove from the left (deleting zero counts). The answer is the largest window seen.

title: Scrambled sightings
statement: Given a text and a short pattern, list every starting index (0-based) where a substring of the text is a rearrangement of the pattern. Print the indices in increasing order, or "-" if there are none.
input: Line 1: the text; line 2: the pattern.
output: Space-separated indices, or "-".
constraints: 1 ≤ pattern length ≤ text length ≤ 10^5; lowercase letters

examples.why: abx, xba, bax, xab are rearrangements.
Every window of two a's matches.

hints: The window length is fixed at len(pattern).
Compare letter counts of the window with the pattern counts as it slides.
approach: Keep letter counts for the pattern and for the current window of the same length. On each slide update two counts and compare the count arrays (26 entries), recording the start when equal.
complexity: O(26 n) time, O(1) extra space

title: Forgiving streak
statement: A habit tracker shows 1 for a day you did the habit and 0 for a day you missed. You may pretend that up to k missed days were successes. What is the longest streak of consecutive 1s you could claim?
input: Line 1: n values (0 or 1); line 2: k.
output: One integer.

examples.why: Flip the zero at index 5 to join 1 1 0->1 1: days 3 to 6.
Any two of the three zeros.

hints: Slide a window and count zeros inside it.
If zeros exceed k, advance the left end.
approach: Expand the right end, counting zeros. While the zero count is above k, move the left end forward (decrementing the count when leaving a zero). The best window length is the answer.

title: All-different week
statement: Among all windows of exactly k consecutive values in which every value is different, find the largest sum. If no such window exists print 0.
input: Line 1: n integers; line 2: k.
output: One integer.

examples.why: Every window has a repeat.

hints: Track counts of values in the window and the number of distinct values.
A window is valid when the number of distinct values equals k.
approach: Slide a fixed window of size k maintaining a count map and the sum. When the map has exactly k keys the window is all distinct, so update the best sum.

title: Patch the fence
statement: A fence is a string of coloured planks (letters). You can repaint at most k planks to any colour. What is the length of the longest stretch of consecutive planks that can be made all one colour?
input: Line 1: the string; line 2: k.
output: One integer.
constraints: 1 ≤ length ≤ 10^5; uppercase or lowercase letters; 0 ≤ k ≤ length

examples.why: "yzzzy" becomes zzzzz with 2 repaints.
No repaints, so only single planks.

hints: A window is fine if length - (count of its most common colour) ≤ k.
The max count never needs to shrink for the window to stay as large as the best seen.
approach: Slide a window while tracking the highest frequency of any letter seen in it. If window size minus that frequency exceeds k, advance the left end by one. The final window size is the answer.

title: Biggest glued number
statement: Given non-negative integers, glue them together in some order to form the largest possible number (as a string of digits). If the result would be all zeros, print a single 0.
input: One line of n non-negative integers.
output: The largest concatenation as a string.

examples.why: 7 first, then 12 before 121 because "12121" > "12112".
Zeros collapse to 0.

hints: Sorting numerically or by string does not work directly.
Order a before b if a+b is greater than b+a as strings.
approach: Sort the numbers as strings with a comparator that puts a before b when a+b > b+a, then join them. If the first character is 0 the answer is 0.
complexity: O(n log n * L) time, O(n L) space

title: Queue jumps
statement: People in a line have ticket numbers and should be served in increasing order. Count the pairs of people (i, j) with i earlier in line than j but a larger ticket number than j: each such pair is a "jump". Print the total.
input: One line of n integers.
output: One integer.

examples.why: Every pair is out of order: 4+... = 3+2+1.

hints: Brute force is O(n^2); think about merge sort.
When merging, an element taken from the right half jumps over everything left in the left half.
approach: Run merge sort; while merging two sorted halves, whenever the right element is smaller than the current left element, add the number of remaining left elements to the answer.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

title: Search the spun dial
statement: A sorted list of distinct numbers was rotated at an unknown point (for example 1 2 3 4 5 became 4 5 1 2 3). Find the index of a target value in the rotated list, or -1, using binary search.
input: Line 1: the rotated list; line 2: the target.
output: An index or -1.

examples.why: 3 is at index 4.
8 is not in the list.

hints: At every midpoint, at least one half is sorted.
Check whether the target lies inside the sorted half; if so go there, else go to the other half.
approach: In each step compare a[lo] and a[mid] to determine which half is sorted, test whether the target falls in that half's range, and discard the other half accordingly.

title: Slowest robot speed
statement: A robot vacuum must clean several rooms with the given sizes. At speed s it cleans s units per hour and works on one room at a time; a room takes ceil(size / s) whole hours (it never starts a second room within the same hour). Find the smallest integer speed that finishes all rooms within h hours.
input: Line 1: room sizes; line 2: hours h (at least the number of rooms).
output: One integer speed.

examples.why: At speed 5: 1+2+3 = 6 hours; at speed 4 it needs 9.
One room of 10 in 1 hour needs speed 10.

hints: More speed never takes more time, so the feasibility is monotone.
Binary search the speed from 1 to the largest room size.
approach: Binary search the speed between 1 and max(size). For a candidate, compute total hours as the sum of ceil(size/speed); if it is ≤ h shrink the upper bound, else raise the lower bound.
complexity: O(n log max) time, O(1) space

title: Split the shipment
statement: Packages with the given weights must be shipped in the given order over d days; each day's truck carries a consecutive group and has the same capacity. Find the smallest truck capacity that gets everything shipped within d days.
input: Line 1: package weights in order; line 2: d.
output: One integer.

examples.why: Groups [4], [8,2], [6,3] have loads 4, 10, 9.
Each day takes one package.

hints: The capacity is at least the heaviest package and at most the total.
For a candidate capacity, greedily pack days and count them.
approach: Binary search the capacity between max(weights) and sum(weights). Feasibility check: walk through packages, starting a new day when the current load would exceed the capacity, and test that the days used ≤ d.

title: Missing seat numbers
statement: Seats are numbered 1, 2, 3, ... forever, but a sorted list of distinct seat numbers is already taken. Print the k-th smallest seat number that is still free.
input: Line 1: sorted taken seats; line 2: k.
output: One integer.

examples.why: Free seats are 2, 3, 6, 7, 8 and the third is 6.
Free seats start 1, 2, ... so the 2nd is 2.

hints: At index i, the count of free seats below a[i] is a[i] - (i+1).
Find how many taken seats are below the answer by binary searching on that count.
approach: Binary search the first index where a[i] - (i+1) ≥ k. If that index is lo, then exactly lo taken seats lie below the answer and it equals lo + k.
edgeCases: k beyond the last taken seat

title: Evenly shareable stretches
statement: Count the non-empty consecutive stretches of an array whose sum is divisible by k. Values may be negative.
input: Line 1: n integers; line 2: k.
output: One integer.
hints: A stretch is divisible by k when two prefix sums have the same remainder.
Count equal remainders with a map, starting with remainder 0 once.
approach: Walk the array tracking the prefix sum modulo k (normalised to be non-negative). For each position add the number of earlier prefixes with the same remainder, then record this remainder.

title: Even heads and tails
statement: A coin-flip log is a list of 0s (tails) and 1s (heads). Find the length of the longest consecutive stretch containing equally many 0s and 1s.
input: One line of n values (0 or 1).
output: One integer; 0 if no balanced stretch exists.

examples.why: The first six flips have three of each.
No tails at all.

hints: Treat 0 as -1 and 1 as +1 so a balanced stretch sums to 0.
Equal prefix sums at two positions mean the stretch between them sums to 0.
approach: Convert 0 to -1 and keep a running sum. Store the first index at which each prefix sum occurs; whenever the sum repeats, the stretch between has length current - first index. Keep the max.

title: Long enough profit run
statement: Find the largest total over any consecutive stretch of at least L elements (L or more) in an array that may contain negative numbers.
input: Line 1: n integers; line 2: L.
output: One integer.

examples.why: 3+4 = 7 beats all longer stretches.
Best is the first two: -1-2 = -3.

hints: A stretch ending at j is prefix[j] - prefix[i] with i ≤ j - L.
Maintain the minimum prefix among allowed starting points while scanning j.
approach: Build prefix sums. For each end j ≥ L track the minimum of prefix[0..j-L]; the candidate is prefix[j] minus that minimum. The maximum candidate is the answer.

title: How many rooms
statement: Meetings are half-open intervals [start, end). Find the minimum number of rooms so that no two overlapping meetings share a room.
input: Line 1: n; then n lines "start end".
output: One integer.

examples.why: At time 2 two meetings run; the one at 4 reuses the freed room.
No overlap at all.

hints: Sort start times and end times separately.
Sweep: a meeting that starts after an earlier one has ended can reuse that room.
approach: Sort starts and ends separately. For each start in order, advance the end pointer while ends are ≤ the start (freed rooms); the rooms in use are starts consumed minus ends passed. Track the maximum.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

title: Slot in a new booking
statement: A sorted list of non-overlapping closed bookings is given, plus a new booking. Insert it, merging with any bookings it overlaps or touches, and print the final sorted list, one interval per line.
input: Line 1: n; n lines of intervals; then one line with the new interval.
output: The resulting intervals, one per line.

examples.why: The new booking fits between the two without touching.
It bridges both existing bookings.

hints: Copy intervals that end before the new one starts.
Then merge all that overlap it, then copy the rest.
approach: Scan in three phases: add intervals ending before the new start, merge every interval with start ≤ new end by widening the new interval, then append the merged one and the remaining intervals.

title: Cancel the fewest
statement: Events are half-open intervals [start, end) and must not overlap (touching is allowed). Find the minimum number of events to cancel so that the remaining events are pairwise non-overlapping.
input: Line 1: n; then n lines "start end".
output: One integer.

examples.why: Keep [1,3) and [3,5); cancel the other two.
Nothing overlaps.

hints: Maximise the number of events you keep.
Sort by end time and greedily keep any event that starts after the last kept end.
approach: Sort by end time; keep an event whenever its start is at least the end of the last kept event. The cancellations are n minus the kept count.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space

title: Fewest stakes
statement: Closed ranges are laid out on a line, and you may drive stakes at integer positions. A range is hit if a stake lies within it (endpoints included). Find the minimum number of stakes needed so that every range is hit.
input: Line 1: n; then n lines "start end".
output: One integer.
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10^5; start ≤ end; values fit in 32-bit

examples.why: A stake at 4 hits the first two; another at 7 hits the last.
A stake at 2 hits the first two; the third needs another.

hints: Sort by right endpoint.
Place a stake at the end of the first unhit range; it hits all ranges that start at or before it.
approach: Sort by end. Place a stake at the end of the first uncovered range, count it, and skip every following range whose start is ≤ the stake; repeat with the next uncovered range.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space

title: Days until warmer
statement: You have a forecast of daily temperatures. For each day, report how many days you must wait until a strictly warmer day arrives, or 0 if no later day is warmer.
input: One line of integers, the daily temperatures.
output: One line with n integers, the waiting time for each day.

examples.why: Day 1 waits 1 day, day 2 waits 2 days, day 3 waits 1, the last never gets warmer.
The first three days all wait for 80; 80 waits one day for 90; 90 has none.

hints: A brute-force scan to the right is too slow for large n; what do days still waiting have in common?
Keep a stack of indices with decreasing temperatures; a new warmer day resolves every smaller index on top.
approach: Keep a stack of indices whose answers are unknown, with temperatures non-increasing from bottom to top. When a day is warmer than the top, pop it and record the index difference. Each index is pushed and popped once.

title: Tidy the path
statement: Given an absolute file path, simplify it: remove repeated slashes and '.' segments, resolve '..' by going up one folder (staying at the root if already there), and drop any trailing slash. The result must start with a single slash.
input: One line, an absolute path starting with /.
output: The simplified path.
constraints: 1 ≤ length ≤ 3000; folder names contain letters, digits, dots (not only dots) and underscores

examples.why: Doubled slashes and . are skipped, and .. cancels a, leaving /home/docs/b.
Going above the root stays at the root: /.

hints: Treat each segment between slashes as an instruction.
Split on /, skip empty and '.', pop for '..', push otherwise; join with / at the end.
approach: Split by '/', ignore empty and '.' parts, pop the stack on '..' when non-empty, push other names. Join the stack with slashes and prefix a slash.
edgeCases: Names like ... that are not special

title: Asteroid clash
statement: Asteroids drift along a line; the sign gives direction (positive right, negative left) and the absolute value the size, all at equal speed. When two meet head-on the smaller explodes, equal sizes both explode, and same-direction asteroids never meet. Print the survivors in order.
input: One line of non-zero integers.
output: The surviving asteroids in original order, or EMPTY.

examples.why: The -5 hits 10 and explodes; 5 and 10 survive.
-5 kills 2 but dies to 10; -12 kills 10; then 3 drifts right: -12 3.

hints: Only a right-mover followed by a left-mover can collide.
Use a stack of survivors; a new left-mover fights the top while the top moves right.
approach: Push right-movers. For a left-mover, repeatedly compare with the stack top if it is a right-mover: pop smaller tops, destroy both on a tie, or stop if the top is bigger. Push the newcomer if it survives.

title: Print queue turn
statement: A shared printer takes the job at the front of the queue; if any waiting job has a strictly higher priority, the front job goes to the back unprinted, otherwise it prints. Given every job's priority and the starting index of your job, report on which print (1-based) your job finally comes out.
input: Line 1: priorities (integers). Line 2: the 0-based index of your job.
output: The 1-based print order of your job.

examples.why: Job 2 has priority 3 and is highest, so it prints first.
Order of printing: job 2, job 3, job 0, job 1, so job 0 is third.

hints: Store (index, priority) pairs so you can recognise your job.
Count down priorities: only the highest-priority jobs print, and among equals they print in queue order.
approach: Simulate with a queue of (index, priority). If the front's priority is the maximum among those waiting, print it and increment the counter; otherwise requeue it. Stop when your index prints.
complexity: O(n^2) worst case time with a max scan, O(n) space
edgeCases: Your job is last with the lowest priority

title: Window peaks
statement: A sensor reports readings and you care about the highest reading in every block of k consecutive readings. Slide the block one step at a time from left to right and print each block's maximum.
input: Line 1: the readings. Line 2: the integer k.
output: One line with n-k+1 integers.

examples.why: Blocks hold 5,4,3,2 as their first elements, each the maximum.

hints: Recomputing the max for every block is O(nk).
Keep a deque of indices whose values are decreasing; the front is the current maximum.
approach: Maintain a deque of indices with decreasing values. Before pushing index i, pop smaller values from the back; pop the front if it left the window. After the first k-1 steps the front's value is the block maximum.

title: Add digit chains
statement: Two non-negative numbers are stored as linked lists of single digits with the least significant digit first. Add them and print the sum in the same format (least significant digit first).
input: Two lines of digits, least significant first.
output: The sum's digits, least significant first.
constraints: 1 ≤ length ≤ 10^4; no leading zeros except the number 0

examples.why: 199 + 15 = 214, written backwards: 4 1 2.
999 + 1 = 1000, written backwards: 0 0 0 1.

hints: Add like on paper, one column at a time.
Keep a carry; at each step add the two digits (0 if a list has ended) and the carry, emit sum % 10, carry = sum // 10.
approach: Walk both lists together, adding digits plus carry and appending sum % 10 to a result list. Continue while either list has nodes or the carry is non-zero.
complexity: O(max(n, m)) time, O(1) extra beyond output
edgeCases: Final carry creates a new digit

title: Rotate the chain
statement: Rotate a linked list to the right by k places: each step moves the last node to the front. k can be larger than the list length. Print the rotated list.
input: Line 1: the list (non-empty). Line 2: k.
output: The rotated list.

examples.why: The last two nodes 4 5 move to the front: 4 5 1 2 3.
4 mod 3 = 1, so one move: 30 10 20.

hints: Rotating by the length returns the same list.
Reduce k modulo the length; find the new tail at position n-k-1, cut there and join the old tail to the old head.
approach: Compute the length n while locating the tail, and set k = k mod n. Close the list into a ring, walk n-k-1 nodes from the head to find the new tail, and break the ring after it.

title: Loop entrance
statement: A linked list may have a loop: its tail links back to some earlier node. Print the value of the node where the loop begins (the first node visited twice), or the word none if there is no loop. The input tells you the tail's target index, but your method should not rely on it.
input: Line 1: node values (distinct). Line 2: tail target index or -1.
output: The value of the loop's entry node, or none.

examples.why: The tail links back to index 2, whose value is 7.
No loop, so none.

hints: First detect the loop with slow/fast pointers.
After they meet, restart one pointer at the head; moving both one step at a time they meet again at the entrance.
approach: Detect the loop with Floyd's algorithm. When slow meets fast, put a pointer at the head and advance both by one node; they meet at the loop entrance. If fast hits null there is no loop.

title: Weave the ends
statement: Reorder a linked list L0, L1, ..., Ln into L0, Ln, L1, Ln-1, L2, Ln-2, ... by relinking nodes (not by changing values). Print the new order of values.
input: One line of integers (at least one).
output: The reordered list.

examples.why: 1, then the last 4, then 2, then 3.

hints: Pulling from the back of a singly linked list is awkward; can you reverse part of it?
Find the middle, reverse the second half, then interleave the first half with the reversed second half.
approach: Use slow/fast pointers to find the middle and split the list, reverse the second half, and merge the two halves alternately, taking one node from each.

title: Longest hallway
statement: Rooms form a binary tree and corridors are the edges. Find the length (in corridors) of the longest simple path between any two rooms; it does not have to pass through the root.
input: One line giving a binary tree in level-order, with null for missing children (children of missing nodes are not listed).
output: The number of edges on the longest path.

examples.why: The path 4-2-1-3 has 3 edges.
The path 6-4-2-5-7 has 4 edges and avoids the root.

hints: A longest path bends at some node; what do you need to know about that node's two sides?
At each node the best bend is height(left) + height(right); track the global maximum while computing heights.
approach: Compute heights bottom-up. At every node update the answer with left height plus right height (in edges or nodes minus one), then return 1 + max(left, right).

title: Shared ancestor
statement: In a binary tree with distinct values, the lowest common ancestor of two nodes is the deepest node that has both of them in its subtree (a node counts as being in its own subtree). Given two values that exist in the tree, print their lowest common ancestor.
input: Line 1: the tree in level-order with null. Line 2: two values p and q.
output: The value of their lowest common ancestor.

examples.why: Both live under node 2, and 2 is their deepest shared ancestor.
4 is under the left child and 7 under the right child, so the split happens at the root: 1.

hints: Where could the answer be if p is found on the left and q on the right of some node?
Recurse: return the node if it equals p or q; if both sides return something, the current node is the answer, else return the non-empty side.
approach: DFS returns a node when it matches p or q, otherwise combines child results. The first node where both children return non-null is the LCA; if only one does, bubble that result up.
edgeCases: One value is an ancestor of the other
Both values in the same subtree

title: Zigzag floors
statement: Walk a binary tree level by level, but alternate direction: the first level left to right, the second right to left, the third left to right again, and so on. Print each level on its part of the line, separated by ' | '.
input: One line giving a binary tree in level-order, with null for missing children (children of missing nodes are not listed).
output: Levels in zigzag order, separated by ' | '.

examples.why: Level 1 is reversed to 3 2; levels 0 and 2 read left to right.
Single-node levels look the same in either direction.

hints: Start from a normal level-order traversal.
Reverse every odd-numbered level (or use a deque and append left/right alternately).
approach: Do a BFS by levels and keep a flag toggling after each level; reverse the level's values when the flag says right-to-left.

title: Even keel
statement: A binary tree is height-balanced if, for every node, the heights of its left and right subtrees differ by at most 1. Decide whether the given tree is height-balanced, ideally in a single traversal.
input: One line giving a binary tree in level-order, with null for missing children (children of missing nodes are not listed).
output: true or false.

examples.why: Every node's subtree heights differ by at most 1.
Node 2 has a left subtree of height 2 and nothing on the right.

hints: Computing height separately for every node is O(n^2) in the worst case.
Return the height from a recursive call, using -1 as a signal that a subtree is already unbalanced.
approach: Post-order DFS returns the subtree height or -1 if unbalanced. If either child returns -1 or the heights differ by more than 1, propagate -1.

title: Honest search tree
statement: A binary tree claims to be a binary search tree: for every node, all values in its left subtree must be strictly smaller and all values in its right subtree strictly larger. Check the claim for the given tree; remember the rule applies to whole subtrees, not just direct children.
input: One line giving a binary tree in level-order, with null for missing children.
output: true or false.

examples.why: Every node respects the bounds set by its ancestors.
6 is the right child of 3, which is fine locally, but it sits in 5's left subtree and is larger than 5.

hints: Checking only parent-child pairs is not enough.
Pass an allowed (low, high) range down the recursion; going left tightens high, going right tightens low.
approach: DFS with exclusive lower and upper bounds. A node must lie strictly within the bounds; its left child gets (low, node) and its right child gets (node, high). Alternatively check that an in-order traversal is strictly increasing.
edgeCases: Values at extremes of the int range

title: Balanced from sorted
statement: Turn a sorted array of distinct integers into a height-balanced BST: choose the middle element as the root of each range, using the lower middle when the range has an even length, and build the subtrees from the two halves. Print the tree's pre-order traversal (root, left, right).
input: One line of strictly increasing integers.
output: The pre-order traversal.

examples.why: Root 3; left half [1 2] has lower middle 1 with right child 2; right half [4 5] has root 4 and right child 5: 3 1 2 4 5.
Lower middle of 4 elements is 2; left [1]; right [3 4] gives root 3 then 4: 2 1 3 4.

hints: Each range of the array maps to one subtree.
Recurse on (lo, hi): mid = (lo+hi)//2, node = a[mid], children from (lo, mid-1) and (mid+1, hi).
approach: Recursively pick the lower middle of the current range as the node, build the left subtree from the elements before it and the right from the elements after it. Output the pre-order of the result.
complexity: O(n) time, O(log n) recursion depth

title: Pair in the search tree
statement: Given the values of a BST (as an insertion order) and a target number, decide whether two different nodes exist whose values add up to the target. Avoid checking every pair.
input: Line 1: insertion order. Line 2: the target.
output: true or false.

examples.why: The two largest values add to 13, so no pair reaches 28.

hints: An in-order walk gives a sorted list.
Collect the in-order values then use two pointers from both ends; or use a hash set during traversal.
approach: Traverse in-order to get a sorted array and run the two-pointer technique, moving the left pointer up when the sum is too small and the right pointer down when too large. A hash set during DFS also works.
edgeCases: Target uses the same node twice

title: Remove from the search tree
statement: Insert values into a BST, then delete one value if it is present. When the removed node has two children, replace its value with the smallest value of its right subtree and remove that node instead. Print the pre-order traversal of the final tree (root, left, right), or EMPTY.
input: Line 1: insertion order. Line 2: the value to delete.
output: The pre-order traversal after deletion.

examples.why: The root is replaced by its successor 60: 60 30 20 40 70 80.
3 has two children; its successor is 6, which takes its place: 8 6 1 10.

hints: Handle three cases: no child, one child, two children.
For two children copy the in-order successor's value into the node and delete the successor from the right subtree.
approach: Recursively search for the value. A node with at most one child is replaced by that child. For two children, find the minimum in the right subtree, copy it up, and delete it from the right subtree.
edgeCases: Delete a node with one child

title: Merge many sorted logs
statement: Several servers each produce a log of timestamps already sorted in increasing order. Merge all of them into one sorted sequence, using a heap that always holds just one candidate per log.
input: k lines, each a non-empty sorted list of integers.
output: One line with all values in sorted order.

examples.why: Repeatedly taking the smallest head: 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 9.
Duplicates stay: 1 1 3 5.

hints: Only the first unused element of each list can be the next output.
Push (value, list index, position) for each list; pop the smallest and push that list's next element.
approach: Seed a min-heap with the first element of every list. Pop the smallest, output it, and push the next element from the same list, if any.
complexity: O(N log k) time, O(k) extra space

title: Live median
statement: Numbers arrive one at a time. After each arrival, report the median of everything seen so far: the middle value for an odd count, or the average of the two middle values for an even count. Print each median with exactly one decimal place.
input: One line of integers in arrival order.
output: One line with the median after each arrival, one decimal place each.
hints: Splitting the data into a lower half and an upper half makes the middle easy to read.
Keep a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, balanced to differ in size by at most one.
approach: Maintain a max-heap of the smaller half and a min-heap of the larger half. Insert through one heap into the other to keep order, then rebalance so sizes differ by at most one. The median is the top of the larger heap or the mean of both tops.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

title: How many meeting rooms
statement: Each meeting has a start time and an end time, and a room is free again exactly at the end time (a meeting ending at 5 and another starting at 5 can share a room). Find the minimum number of rooms needed to hold all meetings.
input: One line per meeting: 'start end' with start < end.
output: The minimum number of rooms.

examples.why: The long meeting overlaps both short ones, but those two do not overlap each other: 2 rooms.
Each meeting starts exactly when the previous ends: 1 room.

hints: Process meetings in order of start time.
Keep a min-heap of end times of rooms in use; free the rooms whose end time is at most the new start.
approach: Sort by start time. For each meeting, pop all end times that are ≤ the start, push the new end time, and track the maximum heap size.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

title: k-th in a sorted grid
statement: A grid of integers has every row sorted left to right and every column sorted top to bottom. Find the k-th smallest value in the whole grid (counting duplicates) without flattening and sorting everything.
input: Line 1: k. Remaining lines: the rows of the grid.
output: The k-th smallest value.
constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ r*c; grid up to 300 x 300

examples.why: Sorted values are 1 2 3 4 6 7 8 9 10, so the 5th is 6.
The smallest value is the top-left cell, 4.

hints: The smallest value is always the top-left cell.
Use a min-heap seeded with the first column (or first row); pop k times, each time pushing the popped cell's right neighbour.
approach: Push (value, row, col) for the first cell of every row. Pop the smallest k times; after each pop, push the next cell in the same row. The k-th popped value is the answer.
complexity: O(k log r) time, O(r) space

title: Least-recently-used cache
statement: Design a cache with a fixed capacity that stores integer key-value pairs. get k returns the value or -1 and counts as a use; put k v inserts or updates a key (also a use), and when the cache would exceed its capacity the key that was used least recently is evicted. Both operations should run in O(1) time. Simulate a list of commands and print the results of the get commands.
input: Line 1: capacity. Line 2: commands separated by semicolons, like 'put 1 10;get 1'.
output: The results of the get commands, space-separated.

examples.why: get 1 gives 10 and refreshes key 1, so put 3 evicts key 2: 10 -1 30.
Capacity 1: putting 2 evicts 1, then updating key 2 to 5 gives -1 2 5.

hints: You need to find a key quickly and also know which key is the oldest in use.
Combine a hash map with a doubly linked list ordered by recency; move a node to the front on every use and remove from the tail on overflow.
approach: Store key to list node in a hash map, and keep the nodes in a doubly linked list from most to least recently used. get and put move the node to the front; when size exceeds capacity remove the tail node and its map entry.

title: Time-travel notebook
statement: Design a key-value store that remembers every value a key ever had. set key value time stores a value at a timestamp (timestamps for the same key are increasing), and get key time returns the value with the largest timestamp not exceeding time, or none if the key had no value by then. Print the result of every get.
input: One line of commands separated by semicolons; keys and values are lowercase-or-digit words.
output: The results of get commands, space-separated.
constraints: up to 10^5 commands; timestamps up to 10^9

examples.in: set a x 1;set a y 4;get a 3;get a 4;get a 0;get b 1
examples.why: At time 3 the latest value is x; at 4 it is y; at 0 nothing existed yet; key b was never set: x y none none.

examples.in: set k v1 10;set k v2 20;get k 15;get k 25;get k 20
examples.why: Time 15 sees v1, time 25 sees v2, time 20 is exactly v2: v1 v2 v2.

hints: For each key the stored timestamps are sorted.
Keep a list of (time, value) per key and binary search for the last time ≤ query.
approach: Map each key to a list of (timestamp, value) pairs appended in increasing order. For get, binary search for the rightmost timestamp ≤ the query and return its value, or none if there is no such entry.
complexity: O(1) per set, O(log m) per get

title: Versioned array
statement: Design an array of n integers, all starting at 0, that can take snapshots. set i v changes one cell, snap saves the current contents and returns the snapshot id (0, 1, 2, ...), and get i id returns what cell i held when snapshot id was taken. Print the result of every snap and get.
input: Line 1: n. Line 2: commands separated by semicolons.
output: One number per snap or get command, space-separated.

examples.why: First snap is id 0; the cell was 5 then. The second snap is id 1 with cell 0 equal to 6, cell 1 still 0: 0 5 1 6 0.
Snapshot 0 saw 0 in cell 1, snapshot 1 saw 9: 0 1 0 9.

hints: Copying the whole array on every snapshot is too slow and memory hungry.
Store for each index a list of (snapshotId, value) changes and binary search at get time.
approach: Per index keep a list of (snap id, value) entries, appended only when a cell changes. On get, binary search the last entry whose snap id is ≤ the requested id, defaulting to 0.
edgeCases: Snapshot id equal to the latest

title: Staircase search
statement: In a matrix every row is sorted left to right and every column is sorted top to bottom. Decide whether a target value occurs anywhere in it, taking far fewer steps than looking at every cell.
input: Line 1: the target. Remaining lines: the rows.
output: true or false.

examples.why: 7 is in the first row.
The values near 10 are 9 and 11, but 10 is absent.

hints: Pick a corner where moving in one direction increases values and in the other decreases them.
Start at the top-right: if the cell is too big move left, if too small move down.
approach: Start at the top-right cell. If it equals the target, done; if it exceeds the target, move left; otherwise move down. Stop when you leave the matrix. Each step discards a row or a column.

title: Zigzag diagonals
statement: Read a matrix along its anti-diagonals (cells whose row plus column is the same), starting with the top-left cell. Diagonals with an even row+column sum are read upwards (from the bottom-left end to the top-right end) and diagonals with an odd sum are read downwards. Print the cells in reading order.
input: One matrix: each line is a row of space-separated integers.
output: All values in reading order on one line.

examples.why: Diagonals: 1 / 2 3 (down) / 5 4 (up) / 6: 1 2 3 5 4 6.
Each diagonal is a single cell, so it is just the row: 1 2 3 4.

hints: Group cells by i + j.
For each sum s, collect cells in increasing row order, then reverse the group when s is even.
approach: Iterate s from 0 to r+c-2, gather cells (i, s-i) that lie in bounds ordered by row, and reverse that list for even s. Concatenate the groups.

title: Is there a loop in the wiring
statement: An electrician has n junctions connected by m wires. A loop exists if you can leave a junction, travel along distinct wires, and come back to where you started. Two wires between the same pair of junctions already form a loop. Report whether any loop exists.
input: First line n m, followed by m lines each with a wire u v.
output: YES if a loop exists, otherwise NO.
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10^5; 0 ≤ m ≤ 2·10^5; u may equal v

examples.why: A chain has no loop.
The triangle returns to its start.

hints: In a forest, joining two nodes that are already connected would create a loop.
Union-find tells you instantly whether two endpoints share a component.
approach: Process wires with union-find; if an edge joins two nodes already in the same set, a loop exists. Self-loops and parallel wires are caught the same way.
edgeCases: Disconnected pieces where only one has a loop

title: Can the course plan work
statement: A degree has n courses, and a line a b means course a must be finished before course b can start. You can take any number of courses in a semester as long as prerequisites are done in earlier semesters. Decide whether it is possible to complete all courses.
input: First line n m, followed by m lines each with a prerequisite pair a b.
output: YES if all courses can be completed, otherwise NO.

examples.why: Take 1, then 2 and 4, then 3.
Each course waits on another in a circle.

hints: A course with no unfinished prerequisites can be taken now.
Repeatedly remove such courses; if you get stuck with some left, there is a cycle.
approach: Use Kahn's algorithm: keep in-degrees, queue zero in-degree courses, and decrement neighbors as courses are taken. If the number taken equals n the plan works.
complexity: O(n + m) time, O(n + m) space
edgeCases: Long cycle hidden behind free courses

title: Split into two teams
statement: A coach has n players and m pairs who cannot stand each other. The players must be split into two teams so that no rival pair ends up on the same team. Decide whether such a split exists.
input: First line n m, followed by m lines each with a rival pair u v.
output: YES if a valid split exists, otherwise NO.

examples.why: Teams {1,3} and {2,4} work.
A triangle forces two rivals together.

hints: Give a start node team 1; its rivals must be team 2, and their rivals team 1.
If a node is ever forced onto both teams, the answer is NO. Remember to start a fresh search in every component.
approach: Two-color the graph with BFS from each uncolored node. Hitting an edge whose endpoints share a color means an odd cycle, so NO.
complexity: O(n + m) time, O(n + m) space
edgeCases: Odd cycle in one far component

title: Smallest valid task order
statement: There are n tasks, and a line a b means task a must come before task b. Among all orders that respect every rule, print the one that is smallest when compared position by position (first number as small as possible, then second, and so on). If no valid order exists print IMPOSSIBLE.
input: First line n m, followed by m lines each with a rule a b.
output: The n task numbers separated by spaces, or IMPOSSIBLE.

examples.why: Start with 3 (smallest free), then 1, 4, 2.
Circular rules, nothing is valid.

hints: A plain queue gives a valid order but not necessarily the smallest.
Among all tasks currently free, always take the smallest number.
approach: Run Kahn's algorithm with a min-heap of zero in-degree nodes. Greedy smallest-first is optimal for lexicographic order; if fewer than n nodes are output there is a cycle.
complexity: O((n + m) log n) time, O(n + m) space
edgeCases: Large number first forced by rule

title: Cheapest delivery route
statement: A courier moves between n depots along m two-way roads, each with a positive toll. Find the smallest total toll to travel from depot a to depot b, or report that no route exists.
input: First line n m a b, followed by m lines each with a road u v w.
output: The minimum total toll, or -1 if b is unreachable.

examples.why: Via 3 costs 4+2=6, via 2 costs 11.
Depot 3 has no roads.

hints: BFS fails because edges have different costs.
Use a priority queue keyed by best known distance and skip stale entries.
approach: Dijkstra's algorithm: pop the closest unsettled depot, relax its roads, and push improvements. Stop or finish and read the distance of b.
complexity: O((n + m) log n) time, O(n + m) space
edgeCases: Direct road is more expensive than a detour

title: Longest dependency chain
statement: A build system has n modules and m dependencies a b meaning a must be built before b; the dependencies contain no cycles. A chain is a sequence of modules where each one directly depends on the previous. Find how many modules the longest chain contains.
input: First line n m, followed by m lines each with a dependency a b.
output: One integer: the number of modules on the longest chain.

examples.why: Chain 1-2-3-4 has four modules.
No dependencies, so every chain has length 1.

hints: Compute for every module the longest chain ending at it.
Process modules in topological order so predecessors are final first.
approach: Run Kahn's algorithm keeping len[v] = max(len[v], len[u]+1) while relaxing edges; initialize every len to 1. The answer is the maximum len.
complexity: O(n + m) time, O(n + m) space
edgeCases: Several roots joining into one node

title: Spreading mold
statement: A pantry shelf grid has M for moldy bread, F for fresh bread and . for empty spots. Each minute, every fresh bread orthogonally next to moldy bread becomes moldy. Find how many minutes until no fresh bread remains, 0 if none to begin with, or -1 if some fresh bread can never be reached.
input: First line R C, then R lines of C characters.
output: The number of minutes, or -1.

examples.why: Minute 1 spoils two slices, minute 2 spoils the last.
The gap blocks the spread, so -1.

hints: All mold spreads at the same time, so start from every M together.
BFS layers correspond to minutes.
approach: Multi-source BFS from all M cells, tracking the minute at which each F is infected; count remaining F's at the end. Return the last minute, or -1 if any F remains.
edgeCases: No mold but fresh bread present

title: Landlocked land
statement: On a map # is land and . is sea. A land cell is landlocked if you cannot walk from it, moving only over land in four directions, to a land cell on the edge of the map. Count the landlocked land cells.
input: First line R C, then R lines of C characters.
output: One integer: the number of landlocked land cells.

examples.why: The 2x2 block in the middle never touches an edge cell via land.
Every cell connects to the border.

hints: It is easier to find cells that can escape than cells that cannot.
Start a flood fill from all border land cells and count the leftovers.
approach: Seed DFS/BFS with every border # cell, marking all land reachable from them. Subtract the marked count from the total land count.
edgeCases: Landlocked cell touching border diagonally only

title: Knight hops
statement: A knight stands on an n by n chessboard and moves in the usual L-shape: two cells in one direction and one cell perpendicular. Find the minimum number of moves from a start square to a target square, or -1 if the knight cannot get there.
input: First line n, second line r1 c1 r2 c2 with 1-indexed start and target.
output: The minimum number of moves, or -1.

examples.why: One L-shaped move from (1,1) reaches (2,3).
The center of a 3x3 board is cut off from every other square.

hints: Squares are nodes and each of the up to eight knight moves is an edge.
BFS from the start gives the shortest move count.
approach: BFS over board squares using the eight knight offsets with bounds checks. Return the recorded distance of the target when reached, else -1.
edgeCases: Tiny board where target is unreachable
Opposite corners of a large board

title: Distance to the nearest well
statement: A village grid contains wells marked 0 and houses marked 1. Walking moves one cell up, down, left or right, and you may pass through any cell. For every cell, print the number of steps to the nearest well. At least one well exists.
input: First line R C, then R lines of C characters 0 or 1 with no spaces.
output: R lines of C space-separated distances.

examples.why: Distances grow by one per step away from the wells at (1,2),(1,3).
Middle houses are one step from a well.

hints: Running a BFS from every house separately is far too slow.
Put all wells in the queue at distance 0 and run one BFS.
approach: Multi-source BFS: enqueue every 0 cell with distance 0, then expand to 4-neighbors, assigning distance+1 the first time a cell is reached.

title: Accounts of the same person
statement: A website has k accounts, and each account lists some email addresses. Two accounts belong to the same person if they share at least one address, and this extends through chains of such sharing. Count the number of distinct people.
input: First line k, then k lines each with a count c followed by c email strings without spaces.
output: One integer: the number of distinct people.

examples.in:
4
2 a@x b@x
1 b@x
1 c@x
2 c@x d@x
examples.why: Accounts 1,2 share b@x; accounts 3,4 share c@x.
No shared emails, so three people.

hints: Use a map from email to the first account that listed it.
Whenever an email is seen again, union the two accounts.
approach: Union-find over accounts plus a hash map email -> account index; union with the stored account on every repeat. The answer is the set count.
edgeCases: Same email twice in one account

title: Islands rising from the sea
statement: A sea is an R by C grid, initially all water. Land rises one cell at a time. After each event, report the number of islands, where land cells joined along sides form one island. An event may name a cell that is already land, in which case nothing changes.
input: First line R C q, then q lines each with a 1-indexed cell r c.
output: q space-separated integers: the island count after each event.

examples.why: Counts 1, 2, 3; then (1,2) bridges (1,1) and (2,2), leaving 2.
Duplicate event is ignored; diagonal cells stay separate.

hints: Offline BFS after each step is too slow.
Add the new cell as an island (+1), then every successful union with a land neighbor removes one.
approach: Keep a union-find over cells and a land set. On adding a cell, increase the count, then for each of 4 land neighbors perform a union and decrement the count if it merged different sets.

title: Cheapest way to wire the town
statement: A town has n houses and m possible cables, each joining two houses at a given price. Choose a set of cables that connects every house to every other (directly or via others) with the smallest total price. Print that price, or -1 if connecting everything is impossible.
input: First line n m, then m lines each with a possible cable a b w.
output: The minimum total price, or -1.

examples.why: House 3 can never be connected.

hints: Sort cables by price and take cheap ones that do not form a loop.
Union-find rejects a cable whose ends are already connected.
approach: Kruskal's algorithm: sort edges by weight, add each edge whose endpoints are in different sets, and sum weights. If fewer than n-1 edges were added, output -1.
complexity: O(m log m) time, O(n) space

title: Are the claims consistent
statement: You are given claims about single-letter variables, each of the form a==b or a!=b. Decide whether all claims can be true at the same time for some assignment of values to the variables.
input: First line k, then k lines each with a claim of exactly four characters like a==b or c!=d.
output: YES if the claims are consistent, otherwise NO.

examples.why: a equals c through b, but a!=c contradicts it.
c can simply differ from the pair.

hints: Equalities create groups; first handle only the == claims.
Then every != claim must connect two different groups.
approach: Union all letters from == claims, then check each != claim: if both letters share a root the system is contradictory. Otherwise it is satisfiable.

title: Words that share letters
statement: A list of lowercase words is split into families: two words are in the same family if they share at least one letter, directly or through a chain of other words. Count the families.
input: First line k, then k lines each with one non-empty lowercase word.
output: One integer: the number of families.

examples.why: abc-cde share c; xyz-zzq share z.
ab and ba share letters; c stands alone.

hints: Comparing every pair of words is O(k²) pairs; avoid it.
Treat the 26 letters as extra nodes and attach each word to its letters.
approach: Create a union-find over 26 letters plus k words; union each word with every distinct letter it contains. Count distinct roots among word nodes.
complexity: O(total length · α) time, O(k) space

title: Fewest arrows
statement: Balloons are stuck on a wall, each covering a horizontal range [a, b]. An arrow shot straight up at position x bursts every balloon whose range contains x (borders included). Find the smallest number of arrows that burst all balloons.
input: First line n; then n lines each with a b.
output: One integer: the minimum number of arrows.

examples.why: An arrow at 6 bursts the first two, an arrow at 12 the last two.
Disjoint ranges need one arrow each.

hints: Sort by right end.
Shoot at the right end of the first unburst balloon.
approach: Sort balloons by right edge. Place an arrow at the current right edge, skip all balloons whose left edge is within it, and start a new arrow at the next uncovered balloon.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space

title: Where to start the loop
statement: A circular road has n fuel stops. Stop i provides g[i] liters, and driving from stop i to the next costs c[i] liters. Starting with an empty tank at some stop, you must drive once around the whole circle in order. Print the 0-indexed starting stop that works, or -1. Inputs are chosen so that at most one start works.
input: First line n; second line n values g; third line n values c.
output: The starting index, or -1.

examples.why: Starting at stop 3 never lets the tank go negative.
Total fuel 9 is less than total cost 10.

hints: If total fuel is less than total cost, no start works.
If the tank fails between start s and stop j, no stop in between can be a valid start either.
approach: Track the running tank; when it goes negative, reset the candidate start to the next stop and the tank to zero. If total gas >= total cost the final candidate is the answer.
edgeCases: Total fuel exactly equals total cost

title: Glue numbers into the largest
statement: Given n non-negative integers, write them one after another in some order to form one long number. Print the arrangement that gives the largest possible value, with no leading zeros unless the whole number is zero.
input: First line n; second line n integers.
output: The largest number as a string of digits.

examples.why: Both zeros give just 0.

hints: Sorting numerically or lexicographically alone fails (3 vs 30).
Compare two strings a and b by whether a+b beats b+a.
approach: Convert to strings and sort with the comparator a+b > b+a descending, then join. If the first character is 0 the result is 0.
complexity: O(n log n · L) time, O(n L) space
edgeCases: Numbers that are prefixes of each other

title: Drop digits to shrink the number
statement: You are given a number as a digit string and a count k. Delete exactly k digits, keeping the remaining ones in order, so that the resulting number is as small as possible. Ignore leading zeros in the result, and print 0 if nothing remains.
input: First line the digit string; second line k.
output: The smallest resulting number without leading zeros.

examples.why: Remove 4, 3, 2 to get 1219.
Remove the 1 to get 0200, which is 200.

hints: A bigger digit followed by a smaller one is a good deletion.
Use a stack: pop while the top is larger than the incoming digit and deletions remain.
approach: Scan digits with a monotonic stack, popping larger tops while k > 0. Trim any leftover k from the end, strip leading zeros, and return 0 for an empty result.

title: Sections without shared letters
statement: Cut a lowercase string into as many consecutive sections as possible so that no letter appears in more than one section. Print the length of each section in order.
input: One lowercase string.
output: The section lengths separated by spaces.

examples.why: Sections are aba, cdc and xyx.
One section holds the only letter.

hints: Record the last position of each letter.
Extend the current section's end to cover the last occurrence of every letter inside it.
approach: Precompute last occurrences. Scan, keeping the furthest last-occurrence seen; when the index equals that end, close a section.
edgeCases: Letter spanning almost the whole string

title: Depth-weighted sum
statement: A nested list is written like [1,[2,3],[[4]]], with integers and lists inside lists. The outermost list has depth 1, lists inside it depth 2, and so on. Each integer is multiplied by the depth of the list that directly contains it. Print the sum of those products.
input: One line with a nested list using brackets, commas and integers (no spaces).
output: One integer: the depth-weighted sum.

examples.why: Empty list adds nothing; 5 sits at depth 2: 10.

hints: Write a function that parses one list at a given depth and returns its contribution.
On '[' call recursively with depth+1; on a number add value·depth.
approach: Recursive descent: parse a list starting at '[', iterating items; integers contribute value·depth, nested lists recurse with depth+1. A shared index tracks the position.

title: Unpack the repeats
statement: A compressed message uses the form k[text], meaning that text is repeated k times, and these blocks can nest, as in 2[a3[b]]. Letters outside any brackets are copied as they are. Expand the message.
input: One compressed string of lowercase letters, digits and brackets, always well-formed.
output: The fully expanded string.
constraints: Expanded length ≤ 10^5; k ≤ 100 (may have several digits)

examples.why: ab2[c] expands to abcc, repeated 3 times.
xyxy followed by z.

hints: Parse until you see ']' or the end of the string.
When you read a number then '[', recurse to get the inner text and repeat it.
approach: Recursive function that accumulates text; on digits it reads the full number, skips '[', recurses to get the inner expansion, multiplies it, and skips ']'.

title: Evaluate a prefix expression
statement: In prefix notation the operator comes before its two operands: + 3 * 2 4 means 3 + (2 * 4). Operands can themselves be prefix expressions. Evaluate such an expression made of integers and the operators +, - and *, using recursion.
input: One line of space-separated tokens forming a valid expression.
output: One integer: the value.
constraints: Up to 10^4 tokens; result fits in 64 bits
hints: Read one token; if it is a number you are done.
If it is an operator, evaluate two sub-expressions in order and combine.
approach: A recursive function consumes tokens from a shared index: numbers return themselves, operators call the function twice for left and right operands.

title: Peaceful queens
statement: Place n queens on an n by n chessboard so that no two attack each other (no shared row, column or diagonal). Count the number of different valid placements.
input: One integer n.
output: One integer: the number of placements.

examples.why: Exactly two solutions exist.
One queen on a 1x1 board.

hints: Place one queen per row, choosing a column.
Track used columns and both diagonals (r-c and r+c) for O(1) checks.
approach: Row-by-row backtracking with sets for columns and the two diagonal directions. Place, recurse, and undo; count placements that fill all rows.
complexity: Roughly O(n!) worst case, O(n) space

title: Find the word trail
statement: A letter grid and a target word are given. Decide whether the word can be spelled by starting at any cell and stepping to horizontally or vertically adjacent cells, never using the same cell twice in one path.
input: First line R C, then R grid rows, then the word.
output: YES if the word can be traced, otherwise NO.

examples.why: s at (2,1), a at (3,1), d at (3,2) spells sad.
Only four cells exist, five letters need five distinct cells.

hints: Try every cell as a starting point.
Mark the current cell as used and unmark it when you backtrack.
approach: For each cell matching the first letter run DFS matching successive letters across unused neighbors; fail fast on mismatch, undo marks on return.
edgeCases: Word that needs to reuse a cell

title: Cut into palindromes
statement: Count the ways to cut a lowercase string into consecutive pieces so that every piece is a palindrome. Cuts at different positions count as different ways, even if the resulting pieces look the same.
input: One lowercase string.
output: One integer: the number of ways.

examples.why: a|a|b and aa|b.
a|a|a, a|aa, aa|a, aaa.

hints: Choose where the first piece ends, then solve the remainder.
Only continue when the chosen prefix is a palindrome.
approach: Backtrack from index i: for each end j where w[i..j] is a palindrome, recurse at j+1. Reaching the end counts one way. Memoizing on i speeds it up.
complexity: O(2^n · n) worst case (O(n²) with memo and precomputed palindromes)

title: Longest rising subsequence
statement: From a list of n integers, pick some of them, keeping their original order, so that each chosen number is strictly larger than the previous one. Find the largest number of integers you can pick.
input: First line n; second line n integers.
output: One integer: the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence.

examples.why: 2, 3, 7 (or 2, 5, 7) has length 3 and nothing is longer.
Equal values are not strictly increasing.

hints: O(n²): len[i] = 1 + max len[j] for earlier smaller a[j].
For O(n log n) keep tails[k] = smallest ending value of an increasing subsequence of length k+1.
approach: Maintain a sorted tails array; for each value binary-search the first tail >= value and replace it, or append if none. The array length is the answer.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

title: Ways to pay exactly
statement: Given n coin values, each available without limit, count the number of different multisets of coins that sum to exactly T (order does not matter: 1+2 and 2+1 are the same). Print the count modulo 1 000 000 007.
input: First line n T; second line n distinct positive coin values.
output: One integer: the number of combinations modulo 1 000 000 007.

examples.why: Cannot make 3 from 2s.

hints: Counting orders instead of combinations happens when the loops are swapped.
Process one coin value at a time in the outer loop.
approach: dp[0] = 1; for each coin value x, for amounts from x to T, dp[a] += dp[a-x]. The coin-outer loop counts each multiset once.

title: Longest shared thread
statement: Two strings are given. A shared thread is a sequence of letters that appears in both strings in the same order, though not necessarily contiguously. Find the length of the longest shared thread.
input: Two lines, each a lowercase string.
output: One integer: the length of the longest common subsequence.

examples.why: a, c, e appear in order in both.
No letters in common.

hints: Define L[i][j] for the first i letters of one string and first j of the other.
If the last letters match, extend L[i-1][j-1]; otherwise take the better of dropping one letter.
approach: Fill a 2D table: L[i][j] = L[i-1][j-1] + 1 if a[i-1] = b[j-1], else max(L[i-1][j], L[i][j-1]). The corner holds the answer.
complexity: O(n·m) time, O(min(n,m)) space with rolling rows

title: Two missing exits
statement: In an access log every badge id appears twice (entry and exit) except exactly two different badges that appear only once. Find both ids and print them in increasing order. Aim for one pass and constant extra memory.
input: First line n (even), second line n ids.
output: The two unpaired ids, smaller first, separated by a space.
constraints: 2 ≤ n ≤ 10^5; ids fit in 32 bits and the two odd ones are distinct

examples.why: 4 and 9 have no partner
8 and 3 are single

hints: XOR of everything equals a XOR b where a and b are the two answers. It is nonzero, so some bit differs between them.
Use any set bit of that XOR to split the array into two groups, each containing one answer plus pairs.
approach: XOR everything to get a^b, isolate its lowest set bit, partition values by that bit, and XOR each group separately.
edgeCases: Answers differ only in the top bit

title: The odd one of triplets
statement: A sensor sends each reading three times, except one reading which was sent only once. Find the reading that was sent once. Plain XOR will not cancel triples, so think about counting bits.
input: First line n (n mod 3 = 1), second line n non-negative integers.
output: The reading that appears once.

examples.why: 9 appears once, 6 and 1 appear three times
2 is the single one

hints: For each bit position, count how many numbers have that bit set.
That count mod 3 is the bit of the answer.
approach: For each of 32 bit positions, sum the bits across all numbers modulo 3; bits with remainder 1 belong to the unique number.

title: Most different pair
statement: Each of n players has a skill signature, a non-negative integer. A pairing is exciting in proportion to the XOR of the two signatures. Find the maximum XOR over all pairs of distinct players (two players may have equal signatures).
input: First line n, second line n integers.
output: The maximum XOR of two elements at different positions.

examples.why: equal values give 0

hints: A brute force over pairs is O(n^2); decide the answer bit by bit from the top instead.
Store prefixes of numbers in a trie (or a set per bit level) and greedily look for the opposite bit.
approach: Insert each number into a binary trie; for every number walk the trie preferring the opposite bit at each level and track the best XOR found.
complexity: O(30 n) time, O(30 n) space

title: Next pattern, same brightness
statement: A light strip shows a pattern stored in an integer; its brightness is the number of 1 bits. Find the smallest integer strictly larger than n that has the same number of 1 bits.
input: One positive integer n.
output: The next larger integer with equal popcount.
hints: Find the rightmost block of ones; you must move one 1 up past a zero.
After moving it, push the remaining ones of the block as far right as possible.
approach: Let c = n & -n and r = n + c (which carries the lowest block up); the answer is r | (((n ^ r) / c) >> 2). Equivalently, find the rightmost '01', swap it to '10', and right-justify the ones below.
edgeCases: n is a power of two

title: The nth smooth number
statement: Call a positive integer smooth if its only prime factors are 2, 3 and 5 (the number 1 counts as smooth). The smooth numbers in order are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, ... Find the nth one.
input: One integer n.
output: The nth smooth number.

examples.why: the tenth listed number is 12
the sequence starts with 1

hints: Each smooth number is a smaller smooth number times 2, 3 or 5.
Keep three pointers into the sequence built so far, one per multiplier, and always take the smallest candidate.
approach: Build the sequence incrementally with three indices i2, i3, i5; the next element is min(2*u[i2], 3*u[i3], 5*u[i5]) and every index that produced it advances (handling duplicates).

title: Show the repeating decimal
statement: Write the fraction a/b in decimal. If the decimals repeat forever, put the repeating block in parentheses, for example 1/3 is 0.(3) and 1/6 is 0.1(6). Terminating decimals have no parentheses and integers have no decimal point.
input: Two integers a and b on one line.
output: The decimal expansion as a string, with a leading minus if negative.

examples.why: 7/4 = 1.75 exactly, with a minus sign

hints: Long division: the next digit depends only on the current remainder.
If a remainder reappears, the digits between the two occurrences repeat; store the digit position where each remainder first appeared.
approach: Perform long division, mapping each remainder to the index of the digit it will produce; when a remainder repeats, insert parentheses from that index onward.
edgeCases: a is a multiple of b

title: Giant Fibonacci index
statement: With F(0) = 0, F(1) = 1 and F(k) = F(k-1) + F(k-2), compute F(n) modulo 1000000007 where n can be as large as 10^18, far too big for a simple loop.
input: One integer n.
hints: Fibonacci can be written as repeated multiplication of a 2x2 matrix.
Alternatively use the doubling identities F(2k) = F(k)(2F(k+1) - F(k)) and F(2k+1) = F(k)² + F(k+1)².
approach: Use fast doubling (or matrix exponentiation) to compute the pair (F(k), F(k+1)) recursively in O(log n) steps, reducing modulo p each time.
complexity: O(log n) time, O(log n) stack

title: Count in base minus two
statement: An odd counter writes integers in base -2, where digit i has weight (-2)^i and digits are only 0 or 1. Convert a (possibly negative) decimal integer to its base -2 representation without a sign. Zero is written as 0.
input: One integer n.
output: The base -2 digits as a string.
hints: Repeatedly divide by -2, but make the remainder 0 or 1.
If the remainder comes out -1, add 2 to it and add 1 to the quotient.
approach: Loop: r = n mod 2 (0 or 1), prepend r, then n = (n - r) / -2 until n is 0.

title: Count the bracket shapes
statement: How many different strings of n opening and n closing brackets are balanced (every prefix has at least as many opens as closes)? Print the count modulo 1000000007. The answers follow the Catalan numbers 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, ...
input: One integer n.
output: The count modulo 1000000007.

examples.why: the empty string

hints: Split on where the first bracket closes: C(n) = sum of C(i)·C(n-1-i).
A direct DP over n up to 1000 is quadratic and fine.
approach: Fill a table C[0] = 1, C[m] = sum_{i<m} C[i]·C[m-1-i] mod p up to n. (The closed form C(2n,n)/(n+1) also works with big integers.)

title: Who is coprime with n
statement: Count the integers k with 1 ≤ k ≤ n such that gcd(k, n) = 1. This is Euler's totient of n. Computing gcd for every k is too slow for the largest n, so use the prime factors of n.
input: One integer n.
output: The count of integers in [1, n] coprime to n.
hints: Start from n and, for every distinct prime p of n, remove the fraction 1/p.
In integer form: result = result / p * (p - 1).
approach: Factorize n by trial division up to sqrt(n); for each distinct prime p set result = result / p * (p - 1).

title: Undo a multiplication
statement: A scrambler multiplies a secret x by a and keeps the result modulo m. To unscramble you need a number y with a·y ≡ 1 (mod m). Find the smallest non-negative such y, or -1 if none exists.
input: Two integers a and m on one line.
output: The modular inverse of a modulo m or -1.

examples.why: gcd(6, 9) = 3, no inverse

hints: An inverse exists exactly when gcd(a, m) = 1.
The extended Euclidean algorithm gives x, y with a·x + m·y = gcd.
approach: Run extended Euclid on (a mod m, m); if the gcd is not 1 return -1, otherwise return x mod m.
complexity: O(log m) time, O(log m) stack

title: Primes in a far window
statement: Count the primes in the closed range [l, r], where l and r can be as large as 10^12 but the range itself has at most 10^6 numbers. A full sieve up to r is impossible, so sieve only the window using small primes.
input: Two integers l and r on one line.
output: The number of primes in [l, r].

examples.why: 1 is not prime -> 0

hints: Any composite in [l, r] has a prime factor ≤ sqrt(r) ≤ 10^6.
For each small prime p, cross out multiples of p in the window starting from max(p², first multiple ≥ l).
approach: Sieve primes up to sqrt(r), then mark their multiples inside the window as composite (never crossing out p itself), and count unmarked values ≥ 2.
complexity: O((r-l) log log r + sqrt r) time, O(r-l + sqrt r) space

title: Two clocks, one moment
statement: Clock A rings on day a, then every m days. Clock B rings on day b, then every n days (days counted from 0, with a < m and b < n). Find the earliest day on which both ring, or -1 if they never do. The moduli may share factors.
input: Four integers a, m, b, n on one line.
output: The smallest non-negative day x with x ≡ a (mod m) and x ≡ b (mod n), or -1.
constraints: 1 ≤ m, n ≤ 10^9; 0 ≤ a < m; 0 ≤ b < n; answer fits in 64 bits

examples.why: x = 8: 8 mod 3 = 2 and 8 mod 5 = 3
x is odd and even at once -> -1

hints: Write x = a + m·k and require a + m·k ≡ b (mod n).
A solution exists only if gcd(m, n) divides b - a; divide everything by the gcd and use a modular inverse.
approach: Let g = gcd(m, n). If (b - a) is not divisible by g, return -1. Otherwise solve k ≡ ((b-a)/g)·inv(m/g) (mod n/g) and return a + m·k, which is below lcm(m, n).

title: Total of all divisor sums
statement: Let σ(k) be the sum of all positive divisors of k. Compute σ(1) + σ(2) + ... + σ(n). Do not factor every number: think about how many multiples each d has.
input: One integer n.
output: The sum of σ(k) for k = 1..n.
hints: Each d contributes d to every multiple of d up to n.
So d contributes d · floor(n/d) in total.
approach: Sum d · floor(n / d) for d from 1 to n.
complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space (O(sqrt n) with block grouping)

title: Bank queue waiting
statement: A bank has t tellers. Customers arrive at known times (sorted) and each needs a known service time. When a customer arrives they take the teller who becomes free first (lowest index on ties); if all are busy they wait. Compute the total waiting time over all customers.
input: First line t and m, then m lines each with arrival time and service duration.
output: The sum over customers of (service start - arrival).

examples.why: third customer waits 3 -> 3

hints: Track the time each teller becomes free.
A customer starts at max(arrival, teller free time).
approach: Process customers in order; pick the teller with the smallest free time (use a min-heap for speed), start = max(arrival, free), add start - arrival to the total, and set free = start + service.
complexity: O(m log t) time, O(t) space

title: Petri dish generations
statement: A petri dish is an h × w grid of cells, # for alive and . for empty; cells beyond the edge are empty. In each generation a live cell with 2 or 3 live neighbours (of 8) survives, a dead cell with exactly 3 live neighbours becomes alive, and every other cell is dead next turn. Print the grid after k generations.
input: First line h, w, k; then h lines of the grid.
output: The grid after k generations, h lines.

examples.why:
a 2x2 block never changes: ##
##

hints: Compute the next grid from the current one into a separate array so updates do not interfere.
Count neighbours with bounds checks.
approach: Repeat k times: for every cell count live neighbours in the previous grid and apply the rules into a new grid.
complexity: O(k h w) time, O(h w) space

title: Where did my card go
statement: A deck of n cards (n even) sits in positions 0..n-1 from the top. A perfect riffle splits it into the top half and bottom half and interleaves them starting with the top half's first card: new order is t0, b0, t1, b1, ... After k such riffles, what position holds the card that started at position p?
input: Three integers n, k, p.
output: The final position of that card.

examples.why: 3 is in the top half (t3) and lands at 6
5 -> 3 -> 6 -> 5, a full cycle of order 3 returns it

hints: Track just one card instead of the whole deck: top-half cards at i move to 2i, bottom-half cards to 2(i - n/2) + 1.
The positions form a cycle; k can be reduced modulo the cycle length, or just simulate with a cycle check.
approach: Apply the position map: p -> 2p if p < n/2 else 2(p - n/2) + 1. Since the map is a permutation the position repeats within n steps; reduce k by the cycle length found when the start position recurs.
edgeCases: p = 0 and p = n-1 stay fixed

title: Three-cell snake
