statement: A snake of length 3 lives on an n × n board (rows and columns 0..n-1, row 0 at the top). It starts with its head at (0, 2), body at (0, 1) and tail at (0, 0). Each command U, D, L, R moves the head one cell; the rest of the body follows, so the tail leaves its cell. Report the 1-based index of the first command that makes the head leave the board (WALL i) or land on its own body (BITE i), or SAFE if all commands succeed. The tail's old cell counts as free after the move.
input: First line n, second line the command string.
output: WALL i, BITE i, or SAFE.

examples.why: the head visits (1,2), (1,1), (1,0), (0,0); the tail left (0,0) long before -> SAFE
head hits column 4 on the 2nd R -> WALL 2

hints: Store the body as a deque of cells, head first.
On each move compute the new head, drop the tail first, then check collision with the remaining body.
approach: Simulate with a deque: compute the new head, check bounds, pop the tail, check the remaining body cells (a set makes this O(1)), then push the new head.
complexity: O(m) time, O(1) space since length is fixed
edgeCases: Moving into the cell the tail just left is allowed
Moving straight back into the neck (L as the first command) is a BITE

title: Falling dominoes
statement: A row of dominoes is given as a string: L means pushed left, R pushed right, . means standing still. Each second a falling domino knocks its neighbour in the direction of falling, but a standing domino pushed from both sides at the same second stays upright. Print the final state once everything settles.
input: One string over L, R and ..
output: The final string of the same length.

examples.why: R at 0 and L at 3 meet: cells 1 and 2 fall towards each other; the last cell is untouched
LL.RR.LLRRLL..

hints: Between two pushed dominoes, three cases: R...L meet in the middle, L...R do nothing, R...R and L...L spread fully.
Alternatively compute a 'force' on each domino from the nearest R on the left and nearest L on the right.
approach: Scan left to right giving each position a force that decays with distance from the last R (reset by L), scan right to left for L, and the sign of the net force gives the final state.
edgeCases: Equal distance between R and L stays standing

title: Calculator with brackets
statement: Extend a calculator to handle round brackets and unary minus (a minus sign in front of a number or a bracket, as in -(2+3) or 4*-2). Operators are + - * / with usual precedence and integer division truncating towards zero.
input: One line containing the expression, spaces allowed.
output: The integer result.
constraints: Length ≤ 10^4; no division by zero; nesting depth ≤ 1000; results fit in 64 bits
hints: Write a recursive-descent parser with three levels: expression (+ -), term (* /), factor (number, bracket, unary minus).
Each level calls the next one down and loops over its own operators.
approach: Recursive descent: expr = term {(+|-) term}; term = factor {(*|/) factor}; factor = '-' factor | '(' expr ')' | number. A single shared position index keeps the parse linear.

title: One careful CSV line
statement: Split a single CSV record into fields. Fields are separated by commas; a field may be wrapped in double quotes, in which case it can contain commas, and a doubled quote "" inside it stands for one literal quote. Empty fields are allowed. Print the field count, then each field wrapped in square brackets on its own line.
input: One line holding the CSV record.
output: The number of fields, then one bracketed field per line.

examples.why: 4 fields: a / b,c / (empty) / d
2 fields: say "hi" and x

hints: Use a state flag for 'inside quotes'.
Inside quotes, a quote followed by another quote is an escaped quote; a lone quote ends the field.
approach: Single pass with an inQuotes flag: commas split fields only outside quotes; a doubled quote inside quotes appends one quote; other characters are appended.
edgeCases: Trailing comma means a final empty field
Empty line is one empty field

title: Look up a setting
statement: A configuration file uses INI format: lines like [section] start a section, key = value lines belong to the current section, and lines starting with ; or # are comments; blank lines are ignored. Keys before any section belong to the global section (empty name). Answer a query written as section.key (or just key for the global section).
input: First line the query, then the config file lines.
output: The value (trimmed of spaces) or MISSING.
constraints: ≤ 1000 lines; keys and sections contain no dots or equals signs; a repeated key keeps its last value

examples.why: name is global, the only name is in section x -> MISSING

hints: Track the current section name while scanning lines.
Split key and value at the first '=' and trim both.
approach: Parse line by line, maintaining the current section; store values in a dictionary keyed by (section, key); finally look up the query.

title: From infix to postfix
statement: Convert an infix expression with non-negative integers, + - * / and round brackets to postfix notation. All operators are left-associative, * and / bind tighter than + and -. Output the postfix tokens separated by single spaces.
input: One line with the infix expression.
output: The postfix expression.
hints: Keep an operator stack. Numbers go straight to the output.
Before pushing an operator, pop operators of greater or equal precedence from the stack to the output.
approach: Shunting-yard: output numbers directly; for an operator pop stack operators with precedence ≥ its own (left associativity) before pushing; '(' is pushed, ')' pops until the matching '('; flush the stack at the end.

title: Depth-weighted list total
statement: A nested list is written like [1,[2,3],[[4],-5],[]] with integers, commas and square brackets. Parse it and output the sum weighted by depth: each integer is multiplied by how many brackets enclose it. So in [1,[2]] the 1 counts once and the 2 counts twice, for 5.
input: One line with a valid nested list (no spaces).
output: The depth-weighted sum.

examples.why: no integers -> 0

hints: Track current depth while scanning characters; no need to build the structure.
When you read an integer, add depth × value.
approach: Scan characters, incrementing depth on '[' and decrementing on ']'; parse each integer (with optional minus) and add value × depth to the total.

title: Unescape then show codes
statement: A string literal contains escape sequences: \n (newline), \t (tab), \\ (one backslash), \xHH (the character with that two-digit hex code), and \ followed by any other character means that character itself. Decode the literal, then print the character codes of the decoded text, separated by |.
input: One line with the raw literal text (without surrounding quotes).
output: The ASCII codes of the decoded characters joined by |.
constraints: Length ≤ 10^4; escapes are valid; decoded characters are ASCII

examples.why: A, backslash, newline -> 65|92|10

hints: Scan with an index; on a backslash look at the next character to decide how far to advance.
For \x, parse the next two characters as hexadecimal.
approach: Single pass with an index: copy normal characters, and on a backslash decode according to the following character, advancing by 2 (or 4 for \xHH).

title: C: linked stack, no leaks
statement: In C, implement a stack as a singly linked list whose nodes are allocated with malloc. Process commands: 'push x' adds an int and 'pop' prints the top value (or EMPTY if the stack is empty). At the end free every remaining node so a leak checker such as valgrind would report nothing.
input: First line the number of commands q, then q commands.
output: One line per pop with the popped value or EMPTY.

examples.why: 7, 4, EMPTY
the last pushed value comes off first -> 2

hints: Each node holds a value and a next pointer; the stack is just a pointer to the top node.
When popping, save the next pointer and the value before calling free on the node.
approach: push mallocs a node and links it in front of the head; pop reads head->value, moves head to head->next, frees the old node; a final loop frees leftovers.
edgeCases: Use after free when reading the value

title: C++: move-only token
statement: In C++, model a unique resource with a move-only class Token (delete the copy constructor and copy assignment, provide move operations). n people numbered 0..n-1 pass it around; person 0 holds it at the start. Each command 'a b' says person a hands the token to person b. If a does not hold it, print ERR and change nothing; otherwise print OK. Finally print 'owner X'. Implement each person as an std::optional<Token> or unique_ptr slot and transfer with std::move.
input: First line n and m, then m lines 'a b'.
output: m lines of OK/ERR then 'owner X'.

examples.why: OK, then person 0 no longer has it so ERR, then OK, owner 2
person 1 does not hold the token -> ERR, owner 0

hints: A moved-from object is valid but unspecified; treat the source slot as empty after std::move.
Deleting the copy operations makes accidental copies a compile error.
approach: Keep slots[i] as optional<Token>; on 'a b' check slots[a].has_value(), then slots[b] = std::move(slots[a]) and reset slots[a]. Track the owner index to print at the end.
edgeCases: Handing over a token you do not hold

title: C++: tree owned by unique_ptr
statement: In C++, build a binary search tree where each node owns its children through std::unique_ptr<Node> (no raw new/delete in your own code, no manual destructor). Insert the given values in order, ignoring duplicates, and print an in-order traversal. When the root goes out of scope the whole tree must be freed automatically.
input: First line n, second line n integers.
output: The distinct values in increasing order.

examples.why: duplicate 2 ignored -> 1 2 4 6
single node

hints: Insert recursively through a reference to the unique_ptr slot: if the slot is empty, assign make_unique<Node>(v).
Recursive destruction of unique_ptr nodes is automatic, but very deep trees can overflow the stack.
approach: insert(std::unique_ptr<Node>& slot, v): create the node when the slot is empty, otherwise recurse left or right; an in-order recursion prints the sorted values.
complexity: O(n log n) average time, O(n) space
edgeCases: Sorted input gives a deep tree

title: Rust: Result and the ? operator
statement: In Rust, write fn parse_line(s: &str) -> Result<i64, ParseError> where ParseError is your own enum with variants Empty and Bad. Return Empty for a blank line and Bad when the text is not a valid integer (use map_err and the ? operator). In main, read n lines, add up the valid ones and count the failures; print the sum and the failure count.
input: First line n, then n lines of text.
output: The sum of valid integers and the number of invalid or blank lines, separated by a space.

examples.why: abc is invalid; 10 + (-3) = 7 with 1 failure
surrounding spaces are trimmed -> 42 0

hints: Trim the line first, then check is_empty before calling parse::<i64>().
map_err converts std::num::ParseIntError into your enum so ? can propagate it.
approach: parse_line trims; empty -> Err(Empty); s.parse::<i64>().map_err(|_| ParseError::Bad)?; main matches on the Result and updates the sum or failure counter.
complexity: O(total length) time, O(1) extra space
edgeCases: Blank lines (blank is Empty, not Bad)
Leading plus sign is valid for parse

title: Go: worker pool
statement: In Go, sum the squares of n numbers using w worker goroutines. Send the numbers on a jobs channel, have each worker read from it with range, and send each square on a results channel; use a sync.WaitGroup to close the results channel once all workers finish. The main goroutine adds up the results and prints the total.
input: First line n and w, second line n integers.
output: The sum of squares.

examples.why: more workers than jobs still works -> 25

hints: Close the jobs channel after sending so the workers' range loops end.
Close the results channel from a separate goroutine that waits on the WaitGroup, otherwise main never stops reading.
approach: Start w workers each doing for x := range jobs { results <- x*x }. A producer goroutine feeds and closes jobs, another goroutine does wg.Wait() then close(results), and main sums over range results.
complexity: O(n) time of work spread across w workers, O(w) goroutines
edgeCases: Deadlock if channels are never closed
